disposition_reason: Narrative review of pesticides, acaricides, antibiotics, metals, particulate matter/microplastics, natural toxins and storage in bee products; metals coverage is a few paragraphs citing other studies, with explicit apiary-siting, monitoring and packaging recommendations. No new honey measurements and no heavy-metal table.
disposition_locator: 'Environmental pollutants' section (md lines 246-276, PDF pp.11-13); 'Improper storage of bee products' (md lines 294-317, PDF pp.13-14); 'Conclusions' (md line 329, PDF p.15)

study.design: review (narrative; no search protocol, no pooling)
study.material_scope: honey, bee-collected pollen (BCP), propolis, beeswax, royal jelly, bee bread (literature)
study.basis: not applicable; the only honey metal numbers restated (Mititelu et al. 2022) are in mg/kg without basis

controls.control: Do not install beehives close to polluting businesses, especially industrial settings highly polluted with heavy metals
controls.outcome: Stated as necessary 'to prevent contamination' of bee products.
controls.locator: section 'Environmental pollutants', md copy lines 254 (approx. article PDF p.11 from _page_N_ image markers)

controls.control: Choose apiary location; consumers should check product source
controls.comparator: A1 high-industrial (refinery) vs A2 low-industrial/moderate agriculture; 144 samples total (12 each of honey types, propolis, soil)
controls.outcome: Romanian accredited beekeepers' hives in a high-industrial area with a refinery (A1) vs a virtually non-industrial, moderate-agriculture area (A2): Pb above acceptable levels in A1, highest in propolis and multifloral honey; Zn high in polyfloral honey and propolis; significantly lower metals in A2 bee products. Review concludes beekeepers should attend to apiary location and consumers should check sources.
controls.locator: section 'Environmental pollutants', md copy lines 276 (approx. article PDF p.12 from _page_N_ image markers)
controls.note: No honey concentrations given for A1/A2 in this paragraph; the 'acceptable level' benchmark is not named.

controls.control: Industrialized-area honey shows elevated Zn and Cu
controls.outcome: Honey from industrialized areas accumulated Zn 3.99-3.09 mg/kg and Cu 2.54-1.03 mg/kg, with lowest Cd 0.07-0.02 mg/kg (as restated by the review).
controls.locator: section 'Environmental pollutants', md copy lines 258 (approx. article PDF p.11 from _page_N_ image markers)
controls.note: Restated values from a cited primary; not extracted as occurrence. Range order printed high-to-low as in source.

controls.control: Urban road traffic particulate contaminates honey
controls.outcome: Metal-based particles from automotive traffic (Fe-based compounds, metallic Zn, barite, antimony oxide) contaminate BCP and honey in metropolitan settings; PM sources include vehicles, pavement/brake/tyre abrasion, smelting, quarrying, metal industries.
controls.locator: section 'Environmental pollutants', md copy lines 264-270 (approx. article PDF p.11-12 from _page_N_ image markers)

controls.control: Bees cannot avoid moderately metal-contaminated forage
controls.outcome: Bees showed no preference against As-, Pb- or Zn-spiked food except at extreme concentrations; they cannot recognise moderate yet dangerous contaminant levels in flowers, so forage location rather than bee behaviour determines exposure.
controls.locator: section 'Environmental pollutants', md copy lines 256 (approx. article PDF p.11 from _page_N_ image markers)

controls.control: Mining, metal-ore/coal processing, phosphate fertiliser, fracking, heavy irrigation/fertilisation and contaminated water as metal sources
controls.outcome: Listed as major causes of metal/metalloid contamination; contaminated water an overlooked bee exposure channel.
controls.locator: section 'Environmental pollutants', md copy lines 252, 262 (approx. article PDF p.11 from _page_N_ image markers)

controls.control: Use honey bees and bee products as bioindicators of environmental pollution
controls.outcome: Honey bees described as reliable/good bioindicators of environmental pollution; potential of bee products as bioindicators 'should be considered'.
controls.locator: section 'Abstract; Environmental pollutants; Future perspectives', md copy lines 13, 262, 321 (approx. article PDF p.11 from _page_N_ image markers)

controls.control: Evaluate bee products for hazardous heavy metals before use as dietary supplements; establish regulatory limits for inorganic pollutants
controls.outcome: Because bee products are heterogeneous and environment-dependent, quality should be evaluated for heavy metals and regulations defining acceptable inorganic pollutant levels should be established.
controls.locator: section 'Environmental pollutants', md copy lines 260 (approx. article PDF p.11 from _page_N_ image markers)
controls.note: Implies absence of harmonised metal limits for bee products; no specific honey ML is cited.

controls.control: Establish and maintain honey monitoring programmes
controls.outcome: 'Honey monitoring programs should be established and maintained' to ensure risk-free consumer use.
controls.locator: section 'Conclusions', md copy lines 329 (approx. article PDF p.15 from _page_N_ image markers)

controls.control: Reduce plastic packaging; develop resistant packaging; attention to packing and storage conditions
controls.outcome: Honey can degrade plastic packaging during long storage (temperature, humidity, light); plastic use should be reduced to minimise micro/nanoplastic migration.
controls.locator: section 'Improper storage of bee products', md copy lines 317 (approx. article PDF p.14 from _page_N_ image markers)

controls.control: Move hives at least 3 km from pesticide-treated agricultural areas
controls.outcome: Beekeepers can reduce residue risk by moving hives at least 3 km away from pesticide-treated areas.
controls.locator: section 'Conclusions', md copy lines 329 (approx. article PDF p.15 from _page_N_ image markers)
controls.note: Pesticide residues, not metals; recorded only because it is the review's one quantified siting distance.

notes: Primary studies cited for metal statements (not re-extracted): Mititelu et al. 2022 (Romania, industrial A1 vs A2 honey/propolis/soil); Bakirci 2019 (Aydin, Turkey; BCP/propolis metals); Klym & Stadnytska 2019 (Ukraine BCP); Topal et al. 2022 (Izmir BCP As/Pb seasonality); Papa et al. 2021a (Po Valley PM in bee pollen/honey); Goretti et al. 2020; Tomczyk et al. 2020 (already in this audit's primary folder); Monchanin et al. 2022; Burden et al. 2019 (see context-dispositions); Costa et al. 2019; Perugini et al. 2011; Porrini et al. 2003; Traynor et al. 2021; Matuszewska et al. 2021. Pollen (BCP) values from Bakirci 2019 (Fe 158516, Cu 7104, Zn 29482, Pb 899, Cd 34 ug/kg) concern pollen, not honey. Candidate primary for direct honey extraction: Mititelu et al. 2022.
contradictions_with_stored_summary: Summary lists metals [Pb, Cd, Hg, As, Cr, Ni] and says urban/industrial bee products show elevated 'Pb, Cd, and Hg'; the source text never mentions mercury, and Cr/Ni appear only in one sentence about propolis/BCP element ranking (Bakirci 2019, md line 258).

Summary says 'Table pages 6-7 provide representative heavy metal concentration data in honey and pollen'; Tables 1 and 2 are pesticide and bee-drug residues and Table 3 is pathogens; there is no heavy-metal table.

Summary says 'Maximum residue levels and EU regulatory standards for heavy metals in honey are discussed'; the source names no EU metal maximum level for honey; it only says regulations 'should be established' (md line 260) and cites WHO permissible limits for BCP.

Summary states 'heavy metals in honey are typically in the range of ug/kg (ppb); pollen concentrates metals at higher levels than honey'; neither statement appears as such; the only honey metal numbers are Mititelu 2022 values in mg/kg.
